checks.title: Time window
checks.detail: We started the time window just before the change, so the requests from before and after it were both in view.

checks.title: The service
checks.detail: We looked at the service the change went to, and found that some of its requests were failing while others succeeded.

checks.title: What they share
checks.detail: We kept only the failed requests, compared every field at once, and found that every one of them had the same ${param.facet.noun}.

checks.title: Cause
checks.detail: We checked that the first failure came after the change began, and that no successful request had that ${param.facet.noun}.

answer.evidence: Every failed request has ${truth.finding}, and no successful one does. ${param.facet.mixed} were mixed, so the ${param.facet.noun} sets the failures apart.

scope.concept: The window has to reach back before the change. A fixed start stays put while you investigate; “the last 15 minutes” moves with the clock.
scope.narration: The change began rolling out at ${incident.rollout_clock} (${incident.rollout_ago}). Start the window a little before then, so you can see the change and the traffic just before it.
scope.reasoning: Starting just before the change puts the healthy traffic from before it next to the traffic after it. A fixed start keeps both in view, however long you take.
scope.evidence: The histogram should start a little before the change.

demonstration.narration: The change began rolling out at ${incident.rollout_clock}. I'll start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}, the five-minute mark before it. A fixed start keeps the change in view, however long we take.
demonstration.evidence: The window now starts at ${incident.window_start_clock}, before the change at ${incident.rollout_clock}. The start is a fixed time, so the first requests after the change can't slide out of view.

drifts.note: You started searching before setting the time window; this step is about choosing when to look.

hints: The briefing says when the change began; the window has to start before that. A fixed start stays put, where the last 15 minutes moves on with the clock.
Click the date box at the top of Discover and type a start date and time followed by “to now”.
Start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}: type “${incident.window_start_typed} to now”. Show me can do it for you.

isolate.title: Look at the service the change went to
isolate.concept: A change reaches one service, so start with that one. A filter pill keeps only one value of a field, so you can look at that service on its own.
isolate.narration: The briefing names the service the change went to. Filter to it: find the field with each request's service, and click the + next to it in its Top values. Then read the HTTP status codes.
isolate.reasoning: A change reaches one service at a time, so that is where its failures would be. Looking at that service on its own shows whether its requests are failing.
isolate.evidence: Only that service's requests remain, some failing and some succeeding.

demonstration.narration: The change went to ${param.incident.service}, so I'll filter service.name to it with the + in its Top values, then read the status codes.
demonstration.reasoning: The window mixes every service's traffic, and a change reaches one service at a time. A filter pill keeps only that one, so its status codes show whether its requests fail.
demonstration.evidence: Some ${param.incident.service} requests fail and others succeed: the http.response.status_code column shows both ${param.incident.status} and 200. The service.name: ${param.incident.service} filter pill keeps only this service's requests. Next, we keep only the failures.

hints: The change reached one service, and the briefing names it (Incident info shows it again). Start with that one.
Open service.name's Top values and click the + next to the service the change went to. Then read the http.response.status_code column.
Filter service.name for ${param.incident.service} with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You filtered on the service ${action.value}. The briefing says the change went to another one (Incident info shows it again).

inspect.title: Look for what the failures share
inspect.concept: Field statistics counts the distinct values of every field at once. A field with one value across all the failures is something they share.
inspect.narration: Switch from Documents to Field statistics. It counts the distinct values of each column for the failures in view. Look for a column about what handled the request (host, endpoint or version) with one value across all of them.
inspect.reasoning: Any field could set the failures apart. Field statistics shows every field's distinct values at once, so you don't have to guess which one to check.
inspect.evidence: One field has a single value across every failed request.

demonstration.narration: I'll switch to Field statistics, which counts the distinct values of every field for the failures in view.
demonstration.reasoning: Any field could set the failures apart, so we scan them all instead of guessing one. A field with one value across every failure is something they share, unless our own filters put that one value there.
demonstration.evidence: Every failed request has the same ${param.facet.field}, while ${param.facet.others} each have several values. service.name shows one value only because we filtered to that service, and http.response.status_code because every failure returns the same error. Each .keyword row repeats the field above it. So the ${param.facet.noun} is the one thing the failures share that our filters didn't put there. The ${param.facet.field} column shows which ${param.facet.noun} it is.

hints: Compare every field at once, rather than guessing which one matters.
Switch from Documents to Field statistics, above the results, and read the Distinct values column for host.name, url.path and service.version.
Open Field statistics and read ${param.facet.field}'s distinct values; Show me can do it for you.
Sum up what the failed requests share, and when the first one happened.
Use the coach's answer form. Give what the failures share, the service, the time of the first failure as Discover shows it, and the comparison with the successes.
Submit what they share, the service, the first failure and the conclusion; Show me shows the reference summary.

goal.title: Keep only the failed requests
goal.concept: To find what failed requests have in common, look at them on their own first.
goal.narration: Keep only this service's failed requests. Find the field that says whether each request succeeded, and in its Top values click the + next to the value for failed requests.
goal.reasoning: With only the failures in view, anything they all share stands out. Successful requests mixed in would blur it.
goal.evidence: A filter pill keeps only the failed requests.

demonstration.narration: I'll keep only the failed requests, with the + next to failure in event.outcome's Top values.
demonstration.reasoning: To find what the failures have in common, we look at them on their own. Successful requests mixed in would blur any pattern.
demonstration.evidence: The event.outcome: failure filter pill keeps only the failed ${param.incident.service} requests, and the hit count shows how many. Next, we look for something they all share.

hints: Look at the failed requests on their own.
Open event.outcome's Top values and click the + next to the value for failed requests. (A range on http.response.status_code from 500 up works too.)
Filter event.outcome for failure with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That keeps the ${action.value} requests. This step looks at the failures on their own.

goal.title: Find when the first failure happened
goal.concept: Sorting oldest first puts the start of a change at the top of the table. Newest first hides it at the bottom.
goal.narration: Sort the results oldest first, and read the time of the first failure.
goal.reasoning: The brief asks when the first failure happened. Discover lists the newest requests first, so the first failure is at the far end. Sorting the other way brings it to the top.
goal.evidence: With only failures in view, the top row is the first failure.

demonstration.narration: I'll switch back to the documents and sort @timestamp oldest first, so the first failure comes to the top.
demonstration.reasoning: Discover lists the newest requests first, which puts the start of a problem at the bottom of a long list. Sorted oldest first, the first failure is the top row.
demonstration.evidence: The first failed request came at ${incident.first_clock}, shortly after the change began at ${incident.rollout_clock}. Like every failure, it has ${param.facet.value} in the ${param.facet.field} column. Next, we check whether any successful request has it too.

hints: Discover lists the newest requests first; the first failure is at the other end.
Open the @timestamp column's header menu and choose Sort Old-New, then read the top row.
Sort @timestamp Old-New and read the first row's time; Show me can sort it for you.

drifts.note: That sorts newest first; the first appearance is at the oldest end.
You sorted by ${action.field}; the first appearance is about time, so sort @timestamp.

goal.title: Check the successful requests
goal.concept: Comparing failed requests with successful ones shows whether what the failed ones share really sets them apart.
goal.narration: Turn the failed-requests filter pill around: click it and choose Exclude results. Then check whether any successful request shares what the failed requests had in common.
goal.reasoning: Every failure shares one value. That explains them only if no successful request has it too.
goal.evidence: The successful requests have other values in that column.

demonstration.narration: I'll turn the event.outcome pill around, to see the successful requests instead.
demonstration.reasoning: Every failure shares one value. That explains them only if no successful request has it. One pill switches between the two sides.
demonstration.evidence: Only successful requests remain, and the ${param.facet.field} column never shows ${param.facet.value}. ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Check whether any successful request shares what the failed ones have in common.
Click the event.outcome pill to open its menu and choose Exclude results. Then read the column the failed requests shared.
Turn the event.outcome pill to Exclude results; Show me can do it for you.
